newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Wider inflation target key to lower NZ dlr - NZIER.
newsitem.headline: Wider inflation target key to lower NZ dlr - NZIER.

text.p: Widening the Reserve Bank's (RBNZ) underlying inflation target band may be the key to achieving a depreciation in the currency without significant economic costs, the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research (NZIER) said on Tuesday.
It said the New Zealand dollar was overvalued and was placing at risk its forecasts of moderate growth over the next five years.

Under the assumption of current economic policy settings, the NZIER forecast growth will rise to 3.3 percent in 1997/98 from 1.8 percent in the year ended March 1997, and then average 2.8 percent in the following three years.

Potential policy changes and the high New Zealand dollar could put those forecasts at risk. The dilemma for the incoming government was how to achieve the necessary fall in the real exchange rate without a current account crisis.
"This dilemma illustrates one of the difficulties of targeting an inflation rate significantly lower than our trading partners," the NZIER said.

If exporters were unable to remain competitive in international markets, the dollar could ultimately depreciate through a current account crisis which would significantly lower growth in the short term.

The nationalist New Zealand First Party, which holds the balance of power after an inconclusive general election in October, wants to scrap the current 0-2 percent inflation band and instead target inflation below that of New Zealand's major trading partners.
NZ First is wrapping up coalition negotiations with both the caretaker conservative National Party and the centre-left Labour Party. An announcement is expected later on Tuesday.

The NZIER said the currency had risen in the last few years by much more than the difference between New Zealand's inflation and that of its trading partners. While the Kiwi needed to fall, it was not clear how this could be achieved under the current inflation target without significant economic costs.

The RBNZ's battle to keep underlying inflation below two percent had pushed New Zealand's short term interest rates to some of the highest levels in the world. The more foreigners invested in New Zealand, the more the currency rose.

"Overseas investors enjoy a one way bet: high interest rates and capital gains as the NZ dollar appreciates. They know the Reserve Bank is unlikely to allow the exchange rate to fall given its inflation target," the NZIER said.
Widening the inflation target might reduce overseas investors' expectations of a continued rise in the currency.
"If investors expect a lower return from investing in New Zealand, the inflow of funds will ease, reducing upward pressure on the exchange rate."

The NZIER said while its forecasts assumed a continuation of current policy, with a second round of income tax cuts being implemented in July 1997 and no changes to monetary policy, some change to policy was likely.
"Both a centre right or left government is likely to review the monetary policy target," it said.
